periods.analysis: Volunteer Hours Logged came in at 1505 hours in 2024-Q3, comfortably above the 1200-hour green target and giving residents visible support during our busiest outdoor season. Because this is the first quarter in this view, we are treating 1505 as the operating baseline for park stewardship, library program support, and recreation event coverage. The strongest lift came from Saturday shoreline cleanups at Mariner Point, teen shelving shifts at Central Library, and senior-center garden crews at Bayview Commons. That mix matters because each logged hour translated into cleaner public spaces, shorter program setup times, and more welcoming facilities for families using them every day.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the Q3 volunteer model by locking in the Mariner Point cleanup calendar and Central Library teen shifts before the next seasonal recruitment window. Extend the resident outcome by adding two trained volunteer leads at Bayview Commons so staff can keep converting enthusiasm into reliable service hours. Use this 1505-hour baseline to set site-level expectations without losing the warm, neighbor-to-neighbor feel that keeps people coming back.

periods.analysis: Volunteer Hours Logged remained green at 1303 hours in 2024-Q4, down 202 hours from 1505 in 2024-Q3 but still above the 1200-hour target. The decline was expected as daylight shortened, waterfront events tapered, and several garden teams paused after the October planting cycle. Even with that seasonal step-down, residents still saw strong support through Winter Reads at North Harbor Library, holiday meal packing at the Alder Recreation Center, and trail leaf-clearing on the Eastbank Loop. The key message is that the volunteer base held together through a lower-availability quarter, which is exactly what a healthy engagement system should do.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping winter shifts shorter and more predictable, especially at North Harbor Library and Alder Recreation Center. Extend capacity by piloting a “two-hour help window” option for corporate teams from the airport logistics district, where Q4 availability is uneven but still real. Track repeat sign-ups from Winter Reads volunteers so they can be invited into spring parks and recreation assignments before schedules fill.

periods.analysis: Volunteer Hours Logged rose to 1490 hours in 2025-Q1, up 187 hours from 1303 in 2024-Q4 and again well above the 1200-hour green target. That rebound tells us residents responded when we connected winter service to visible outcomes: restored library tutoring tables, safer trail edges, and smoother youth league registration days. The Harbor Helpers orientation cohort in February, with sessions at Central Library and Westport Recreation Center, helped convert first-time volunteers into scheduled teams rather than one-time drop-ins. We are seeing the benefit of treating volunteers not as extra hands, but as partners in making public spaces feel cared for.
periods.recommendations: Sustain momentum by repeating the Harbor Helpers orientation twice in 2025-Q2, with one evening session and one Saturday session to fit working families. Extend the outcome by assigning each new cohort to a specific resident-facing result, such as summer reading setup, soccer field readiness, or senior lunch check-in support. Keep the Q1 rebound visible to volunteers by sharing simple before-and-after service notes after each shift.

periods.analysis: Volunteer Hours Logged reached 1722 hours in 2025-Q2, up 232 hours from 1490 in 2025-Q1 and the highest point in the arc so far. The green result reflects both seasonality and good operating discipline: spring park workdays on Routes P-4 and P-7, library summer-reading prep, and volunteer marshals for the Harborview 10K all landed in the same quarter. Residents felt this as cleaner playgrounds before school let out, better-supported branch library events, and safer, friendlier public gatherings. The scale is encouraging, but the lesson is not just more hours; it is matching the right volunteers to the moments residents most notice.
periods.recommendations: Sustain this high-water mark by preserving the Q2 sequence: parks workdays first, summer-reading prep second, and special-event marshaling with trained leads. Extend the model by creating a shared volunteer roster between Parks, Recreation, and Libraries so a resident who helps at the Harborview 10K can be invited into July reading events or August trail days. Protect quality by capping new event assignments at the number of trained lead volunteers available, not just the number of people willing to sign up.

periods.analysis: Volunteer Hours Logged was 1465 hours in 2025-Q3, down 257 hours from 1722 in 2025-Q2 but still solidly green above the 1200-hour target. The drop is a reasonable reset after a very strong spring, with summer travel, heat advisories, and fewer school-based volunteer groups affecting availability in July and August. Even so, the department maintained strong resident-facing coverage through splash-pad ambassadors at Seaside Park, youth art assistants at East Harbor Library, and litter teams along the Ferrywalk after weekend peaks. This quarter shows a maturing program: we can absorb seasonal softness without slipping below standard.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green performance by keeping heat-adjusted morning shifts for parks and waterfront assignments in the Q3 playbook. Extend engagement by building a standing “Back-to-School Service Week” with the school district and library branches, aimed at teens who need structured civic hours before fall activities begin. Watch the July volunteer dip by confirming at least 300 hours of pre-scheduled branch and park coverage before the end of each June.

periods.analysis: Volunteer Hours Logged remained green at 1363 hours in 2025-Q4, down 102 hours from 1465 in 2025-Q3 and still above the 1200-hour target. This was a smaller seasonal decline than the prior year’s Q3-to-Q4 movement, which suggests the winter operating changes are helping. Residents benefited from dependable support at the Southside StoryWalk installation, the Harbor Lights recreation events, and food-drive sorting in partnership with the downtown faith coalition. The number is lower than our spring peak, but the service is steadier and more intentional than it was a year ago.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the improved winter floor by repeating the shorter-shift calendar and confirming holiday event captains by October 15. Extend the Southside StoryWalk model to one additional branch service area, pairing library volunteers with parks maintenance staff for setup, wayfinding, and weekly condition checks. Use the smaller 102-hour decline as evidence to keep investing in winter volunteer design, not as a reason to coast.

periods.analysis: Volunteer Hours Logged increased to 1489 hours in 2026-Q1, up 126 hours from 1363 in 2025-Q4 and again comfortably green against the 1200-hour target. The rebound nearly matches 2025-Q1’s 1490 hours, which tells us the program has built a reliable first-quarter rhythm. Crews and volunteers supported the Rain Garden Refresh at Civic Plaza, tax-help greeters at Central and North Harbor libraries, and youth basketball tournament operations at Westport Recreation Center. For residents, that meant easier access to services, better-maintained shared spaces, and public programs that felt organized rather than stretched.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the reliable Q1 pattern by pre-booking Rain Garden Refresh and tax-help greeter roles as recurring annual assignments. Extend the resident benefit by training recreation volunteers in crowd-flow and accessibility support before the youth basketball tournament schedule is finalized. Maintain a simple retention dashboard for volunteers who served in both 2025-Q1 and 2026-Q1, then personally invite them into Q2 high-demand roles.

periods.analysis: Volunteer Hours Logged reached 1721 hours in 2026-Q2, up 232 hours from 1489 in 2026-Q1 and just one hour below the 1722-hour high point from 2025-Q2. This is a very strong green result, and the repeatable 232-hour Q1-to-Q2 lift shows that our seasonal ramp is now predictable. The quarter was powered by Spring into Service park days on the Bluff Trail and P-9 playground corridor, expanded summer-reading packet assembly at three branches, and trained event volunteers for the Seaport Family Festival. Residents saw the payoff in cleaner, safer, better-staffed public experiences at exactly the time demand rises.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the Q2 operating formula by reserving Spring into Service dates, branch packet-assembly blocks, and Seaport Family Festival volunteer roles before the close of Q1 each year. Extend the success by creating a cross-trained lead pool of 25 volunteers who can move between parks, libraries, and recreation events when weather or attendance shifts. Keep the tone personal: send site-specific thank-you notes that name the resident outcome, because that is what turns 1721 hours into lasting civic trust.

periods.analysis: Volunteers logged 1,370 hours, above the 1,200-hour target but below June’s recorded 1,721-hour spring peak. The seasonal decline has not put participation below plan.
periods.recommendations: Retain trained volunteers for fall branch and park assignments, with named backups for activities affected by weather or site access.
